title: AllToAll Exchanges at Scale
summary: Compare the scaling constraints of AllToAll and AllReduce by analyzing logical connection density and network bisection contention.

sections: Dynamic routing and expert imbalance in MoE AllToAll

blocks.md:
This lesson follows **AllToAll Exchanges at Scale** in *Collective Communication* (Vol II). By the end you should be able to:

- Compare the scaling constraints of AllToAll and AllReduce by analyzing logical connection density and network bisection contention
- Distinguish full-duplex bidirectional link capability from multi-destination injection bandwidth limits

blocks.source: Vol II, Collective Communication, § AllToAll Exchanges at Scale
blocks.md: Hierarchy, in-network reduction, and rail alignment were all developed for AllReduce, whose uniform payload lets every rank follow the same schedule. In a mixture-of-experts model with 64 experts distributed across 8 GPUs (8 experts per GPU), or in the sharded embedding tables of a later section, a gating network or lookup table assigns each input to a specific destination rank.

blocks.title: Map of the section
blocks.md:
The section is organised as:

- Dynamic routing and expert imbalance in MoE AllToAll
- AllToAll schedule selection

Pay attention to: AllToAll vs AllReduce scaling: logical peer count versus injection, reception, bisection, and startup bounds; Physical injection link sharing during concurrent peer transfers.

questions.q: Why can MoE token routing with AllToAll encounter contention and tail-latency limits even when its per-worker payload is smaller than that of a dense AllReduce?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. AllToAll has $N(N-1)$ potential directed peer relationships, so placement, routing, and load imbalance matter as well as total bytes. With a fixed total $M$-byte input per rank, uniform AllToAll sends $(N-1)M/N$ bytes per rank, not a quadratic volume. Traffic can still contend on a limited bisection or overloaded expert. The operation does not inherently require TCP or FP32.
questions.hint: Think about: compare the scaling constraints of AllToAll and AllReduce by analyzing logical connection density and network bisection contention.
options: AllToAll transfers more total bytes per GPU than AllReduce, requiring each GPU to send \$2(N-1)M$ bytes instead of \$2 \frac{N-1}{N} M$ bytes.
AllToAll exchanges distinct payloads among many peers; routing skew and concurrent cross-fabric transfers can concentrate traffic on shared links and destinations.
AllToAll cannot execute over InfiniBand fabrics and must fall back to host CPU TCP/IP socket emulation.
AllToAll mandates single-precision FP32 representation, preventing BF16 or FP16 tensor transfers across remote experts.

questions.q: In a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model where tokens are routed across 8 GPUs using full-duplex InfiniBand NDR (50 GB/s per port), issuing 7 concurrent peer transfers allows the GPU to achieve an aggregate outgoing transmission rate of \$7 × 50 GB/s = 350 GB/s.
questions.explanation: False. Full-duplex communication allows a network interface card (NIC) to send and receive simultaneously at line rate (50 GB/s in each direction), but it does not multiply the physical injection bandwidth of a single port across multiple concurrent destinations. All concurrent outgoing peer streams share the same physical 50 GB/s injection link, meaning total outgoing data must serialize through that single port. The aggregate outgoing transmission rate remains bounded by the 50 GB/s link capacity.
